clips.text: First, the baseline. Give your AI a Search Console export of clicks and impressions by page, plus the generative AI report, and it groups the pages by type and gives you a table to compare against once December's update has finished. Second, the pages answering complex questions. Give it your list of pages that answer long, multi-part questions, and ask it to check each one for when it was last substantially updated, whether claims are sourced, and whether a named author is shown. It hands back a ranked list of pages to fix before the rollout. And the freeze itself stays with a person, because someone has to decide what can wait. But AI can watch the dashboard feed and tell the team the day the rollout starts. The prompts are in the show notes.

clips.linkedin:
Google's new Search Console feedback button sounds like an appeal. It isn't.

Google pre-announced its December 2026 core update on 24 November, and alongside it added a feedback route in Search Console for verified site owners.

In this clip Hannah explains why that route isn't an appeal. Google says feedback doesn't lead to manual ranking adjustments for individual URLs, and engineers review it in aggregate. The useful part for a marketing lead is the warning itself, because it lets you keep a migration or a big content prune out of the update window and read the results cleanly.

The job to hand to AI is the baseline. Give it your Search Console export by page and the generative AI report, and it gives back a table by page type to check after the update.

The podcast voices are AI-generated.

Full episode and article at https://manual-focus.co.uk/blog/google-pre-announced-core-update-ranking-hub/
clips.text: Here's where I'd start as a head of SEO. The feedback button sounds like an appeal. Is it? No, and Google says so plainly. Feedback doesn't lead to manual ranking adjustments for individual URLs. Engineers review it in aggregate to spot systemic problems. So it helps with a pattern across a type of page, not with getting your own traffic back. Then the real value is the warning. If you know an update's coming, you can keep a migration or a big content prune out of the window and read the results cleanly afterwards.
